opus-5.5.text:
I think of mathematics and English as two languages with very different jobs, and moving between them has shaped how I think.

English, or any natural language, is wonderfully flexible. It's ambiguous and full of context and connotation. You can say one sentence and mean three things, and that's part of its beauty. Poetry, storytelling and persuasion all live in that ambiguity.

Mathematics is almost the opposite. It's a language designed to remove ambiguity. When you write a definition or a theorem, every word has to mean exactly one thing. "Continuous" or "compact" isn't a vibe, it's a precise contract. In a way, math is what you get when you take a natural language and keep tightening it until nothing can slip through.

What I find most interesting is the space between them. When mathematicians actually do research, we don't think in formal symbols. We think in pictures, analogies and half-English intuitions like "this object wants to collapse here" or "this argument is basically a pigeonhole trick." Then the hard work is translating that intuition into rigorous language. Communicating it to other people means translating back again, writing a paper or giving a talk that a human can follow. So doing mathematics is constantly translating between a fuzzy, human language and a precise, formal one.

That's also why I find the current moment in AI so exciting. Large language models are very good at the English side: fluent, intuitive, sometimes too confident. Formal languages like Lean are the extreme of the mathematical side: a computer checks every step, and nothing is accepted on vibes. Bringing those together, so a system can have intuition in natural language and also verify its reasoning formally, feels like bridging the two languages in a new way.

So for me they aren't rivals. English is where ideas are born and shared, and mathematics is where they're held to account. You need both to do anything really meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response describes mathematics and English as distinct languages and says mathematics tightens natural language, but it does not propose that mathematics is a subset of English.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts mathematical precision with ordinary English ambiguity, but does not state that theorem-formulating words have a different probability distribution in mathematical discourse.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because I grew up thinking of them as two completely separate worlds, and now I see them as almost the same thing.

When I was a kid in Shanghai, math was the thing I was "good at" and English was the thing I had to work on. Math felt like it belonged to me, and English felt like it belonged to someone else. But when I got to MIT and then Stanford, and especially when I started working on AI for mathematics with Axiom, I realized something: mathematics is a language. It has grammar, it has vocabulary, it has idioms. A proof is a piece of writing. The difference is that mathematics is a language where ambiguity is not allowed, and English is a language where ambiguity is the whole point.

So I'd say the relationship is this. English, or any natural language, is how humans communicate intuition. When a mathematician explains why a theorem is true, they don't start with symbols. They say, "think of it like this," or "the key idea is." That's English doing the work of transferring understanding from one mind to another. Then formal mathematics is the compression of that intuition into something that can be checked, that cannot be misunderstood.

What's fascinating to me right now is that large language models learned mathematics through English. They read millions of pages of humans explaining math to each other in natural language. So the model's understanding of math is actually mediated by English, in a way that's very human. And the hard problem we work on is the translation step: going from the informal English argument to the formal, verified proof. That gap is exactly where most human mathematicians also struggle. Writing a proof that convinces your colleague is one skill. Writing a proof that convinces a machine, with no gaps, is a different skill.

I also think, honestly, that being bilingual helped me as a mathematician. When you grow up switching between Chinese and English, you learn early that the same idea can have many surface forms, and that the idea is not the words. That's the core instinct in mathematics too. You learn to see that two problems that look totally different are secretly the same structure. So in some sense, learning English was my first training in abstraction.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematics and English are both ways of expressing ideas, but they give you different kinds of freedom. In mathematics, you want to make your assumptions explicit and your reasoning precise, so someone else can follow each step. In English, ambiguity can sometimes be valuable—a sentence can carry several meanings or make you feel something that’s difficult to state directly.

But there’s also a lot of creativity in mathematics and a lot of structure in writing. A good proof and a good essay both guide a reader toward an understanding. You have to decide what to introduce first, what connections to make, and what to leave out. So I see them as complementary ways of learning to think and communicate.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes mathematics and English as complementary ways of expressing ideas, not mathematics as a subset of English.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematics and English are both ways of expressing ideas, but they ask us to be precise in different ways. In mathematics, you define your terms and build an argument step by step. In English, meaning also comes through tone, context, and the associations a word carries.

What connects them for me is the challenge of making a complicated idea clear. A mathematical proof can be elegant because you suddenly see why something must be true. A piece of writing can give you that same feeling—someone has found just the right way to say something, and it clicks.

r001.rationale: The response describes mathematics and English as distinct but connected ways of expressing ideas; it does not claim mathematics is a subset of English.

r002.rationale: The response mentions mathematical terminology and English meaning generally, but says nothing about the probability distribution of theorem words versus ordinary English.
